Alignment across all 744 common adoptions

Reading the table from the RCF thread

The workbook's own summary, reproduced by the pipeline. The 106, and every "identical" figure in this row of tiles, use column S of the workbook (Parallel degree of equivalence) exactly as the table does.

How the 70 candidate additions are derived

CEN-CENELEC records equivalence in two columns that rarely overlap: column S (Parallel degree of equivalence) for ISO/IEC documents processed in parallel under the Vienna and Frankfurt agreements, and column V (Degree of Equivalence) for documents borrowed from ISO, IEC or BSI (columns T and U). The table's 279 "unidentified" rows are those with column S blank. Applying the same three tests to column V gives the 70.

By sector

Sector of each standard, using the CEN-CENELEC sector classification applied to both the SCC and CEN-CENELEC adoptions, split by the international source organisation.

By responsible committee

The CEN or CENELEC technical body holding the European work item, with its ISO/IEC mirror committee.

Standards families

Most of the list arrives in clusters: multi-part series adopted together on both sides. Each chip is one ISO/IEC series; the number is how many parts or amendments are on the list.

Adoption lag after the ISO/IEC edition

Years between the international edition and each regional or national adoption. Europe votes in parallel under the Vienna and Frankfurt agreements, so its lag is usually zero.

Lag by sector

Median years from ISO/IEC publication to adoption, per sector.

When Canada adopted

Publication year of the Canadian adoption. A reaffirmation (R20xx) keeps an older adoption current without a new edition.

When the ISO/IEC edition was published

Edition year of the underlying international document.

Do the shared standards carry regulatory weight?

Two lenses. Canada: mentions of each standard's document number in every consolidated federal Act and regulation (Justice Laws XML mirror). EU: citations in the Official Journal lists of harmonised standards, which confer presumption of conformity with EU product legislation. Provincial and territorial regulations, and references made only through the Canadian Model Codes (for example the Canadian Electrical Code), are not captured.
